transfer.title: Transfer case · the textbook insulin pump
transfer.text: The textbook's insulin pump. Hazard: insulin is delivered when blood sugar is already low. The sensor reading is correct. This is a different hazard from the controller case.
transfer.source: Source slides 19 and 32 (insulin pump risks and requirements)
transfer.question: Which safety requirement controls the low-sugar hazard, and how would you verify it?
transfer.answer: The pump shall not deliver insulin when the measured sugar level is below the set threshold. It shall raise an alarm instead. Verify with tests that feed low readings and check that no dose is delivered.
transfer.answerKey: no delivery below the threshold plus an alarm

X01.commonError: Students label every medical system “primary” safety-critical. Keep primary (software failure directly causes harm) and secondary (software misleads a person) apart.
X01.question: Can a program obey its specification and still be unsafe?
X01.answer: Yes. The specification may leave out a hazardous condition. Conformance only supports the specified behaviour, not every condition of use.

X02.concept: four ways a reliable system is unsafe
X02.answerKey: define the hazard first, then compare behaviour with the requirement
X02.commonError: Students answer “test more” for all four causes. Only dormant faults are mainly a testing problem; a missing requirement cannot be found by more tests of the written ones.

X02A.answerKey: hazard: occupied zone unprotected; accident: barrier strikes
X02A.commonError: Students use hazard and accident as one word. Draw hazard → accident → damage and ask where the repeated commands sit: a hazardous condition before any harm.

lists.title: Risk reduction strategies
items: Hazard avoidance
Hazard detection and removal
Damage limitation

X02A.takeaway: A hazard is a condition and an accident is the harm; safety engineering breaks the path between them.

X03.commonError: First drafts write “make it safe” as the requirement. Nobody can verify it. Insist on the hazardous condition, the required response and a named verification.

lists.title: Hazard analysis techniques
items: Inductive, bottom-up: start from a possible failure and find the hazards it could cause
Deductive, top-down: start from a hazard and work out its causes

CHECK1.commonError: Students treat “all routine tests passed” as evidence for the untested obscured-sensor case. Ask which condition the tests actually covered.
bullets: A sensor is obscured, but the controller continues its specified routine.
Separate conformance, hazardous condition and possible accident.
Write a claim with its limits and name the missing evidence.

X04.answerKey: hazard, consequences, likelihood evidence, reduction options and justification
X04.commonError: Students invent a probability to place the hazard in a region. The chapter says estimates are relative; stop any number that has no source.

X05.answerKey: shared supply is a common cause; no multiplication
X05.commonError: Students believe an AND gate proves the two causes are independent. Ask what happens to the gate when both checks read the same sensor.

lists.title: Fault-tree analysis
items: A deductive, top-down technique
Put the hazard at the root and find the system states that lead to it
Link the states with AND or OR conditions
Aim to minimise the number of single causes of failure

X06.answerKey: detection, inhibited command and behaviour when detection fails
X06.commonError: Most first drafts forget the behaviour when the sensor is unavailable. Point to SR1 and SR2 side by side: the textbook already has the cumulative lesson.

X09.answerKey: executed verification record with version and reviewer
X09.commonError: Students point to the control description as proof the control was checked. Only an executed verification record, with version and reviewer, shows execution.
X09.concept2: traceable change of a protection rule
X09.answerKey2: changed requirement, reviewed design, version, verification result, reviewer
X09.question: Which hazard-log entry proves that a proposed control was actually checked?
X09.answer: A linked record of an executed verification: version, conditions, outcome and reviewer. The control description alone does not show execution.
X09.question2: What evidence should a changed protection rule leave behind?
X09.answer2: The changed requirement and its hazard link, the reviewed design, the software version, the verification result and the responsible reviewer.

CHECK2.answerKey: shared input, power, assumption or bypass
CHECK2.commonError: Pairs claim full independence between two protection paths. Ask what evidence would falsify it: a shared sensor, supply or assumption.
bullets: Compare a software-only check with a separately monitored protective path.
Identify one common cause and one cost or usability trade-off.
Add the mechanism, why it supports your claim, and what you are unsure of.

R18.commonError: Students take a clean model check as proof about the physical sensor. The check covers the model; sensor behaviour needs its own evidence.

D12.commonError: Students expect static analysis to find a missing requirement. It can catch an unchecked input or an overflow, not a requirement nobody wrote.

lists.title: Levels of static analysis
items: Characteristic error checking: patterns typical of the language
User-defined error checking: rules the team adds
Assertion checking: formal assertions in the code

B01.answerKey: argument linking evidence to a scoped claim
B01.commonError: Students present a folder of test reports as the safety case. Ask for the argument: this claim, this evidence, and why it is enough for this scope.
B01.title: A safety case connects evidence to a claim with limits

X10.concept: every path to the unsafe exit
X10.commonError: Students extend the single-command argument to repeated commands in their heads. Make them say the cumulative claim out loud; it was never written.

AISYS.concept: missing cumulative requirement and its checker
AISYS.answerKey: reject commands that take the total over the limit; safe state on lost sensing
AISYS.commonError: Students look for the row where a single command failed its check. None did. The first unsafe row is C3, where the total passes 10 while every check passed.
AISYS.answer: Requirement: the controller shall reject any command that takes the total within a stated window above the modelled limit. This holds whatever proposed the command. On loss of sensing, it enters a defined safe state and accepts no assistant sequence. Verification: test many small commands, including sequences built to probe the bound, and loss-of-sensing cases. Where feasible, model-check them too. Record version, conditions and reviewer in the hazard log. Neither step depends on the assistant being right. Both depend on the checker seeing every command and on its own sensing. The window and limit shown are illustrative. An optimiser that exploits what the rules forgot is doing specification gaming.
AISYS.takeaway: Every command passed its check, yet the total still left the modelled limit.

APPLY.answerKey: restrict assistant sequences until the cumulative limit is verified
APPLY.commonError: Students ask the assistant to “be more careful”. Reject that: the control must be enforced outside the assistant, with its own verification.
APPLY.answer: A defensible revision responds to the changed assumption, keeps missing evidence visible and names a responsible role. The cumulative limit must hold whatever proposes the commands. Until it is specified and verified, restrict or withdraw assistant sequences. Tell the operators why.

stations.answerKey: pilot record covers single commands only
stations.think: Devices down. What claim does the pilot record support?
stations.pair: Name one assumption and one given fact you need to support your answer.
stations.write: Write your claim and its evidence. Mark any test you only propose as proposed.
stations.hint: Name the service or property first. Use a source definition and the given facts. Ask which missing fact would change your claim. Decide whether the assistant's clean pilot record counts as evidence.
stations.note: Think without devices, then pair. Choosing when not to use technology is part of using it well. Use the same card; nobody is marked on field length or a timer.
stations.answer: An answer with limits separates the given facts from the needed evidence. A source explanation supports a mechanism. It does not prove the fictional deployment passed a test. The clean pilot record shows only that each command passed the per-command check. It says nothing about cumulative actuation or loss of sensing. The argument never covered those.

criteria.name: Names the mechanism
levels: Names the chapter mechanism that decides the case and says how it applies.
Names a mechanism but does not connect it to the case facts.
No chapter mechanism, or the wrong one.

criteria.name: Uses only the given facts
levels: Every statement rests on a given fact or is marked as an assumption.
Mostly given facts, but one invented or unmarked assumption.
Relies on facts the case does not give.

criteria.name: Evidence another person can check
levels: Names evidence a second engineer could inspect, and marks proposed tests as proposed.
Names evidence, but it is vague or its status is unclear.
Opinion or confidence instead of evidence.

rubric.marks: 2 marks per criterion, 6 in total. Not graded in class. The same reasoning earns the assignment points.

strong.text: The pilot record supports one claim: each single command stayed within its limit. It says nothing about the total over a window or about a lost sensor. Evidence still needed: a test of repeated sequences and a loss-of-sensing test, both proposed.
strong.why: Names the mechanism (per-command limit), uses only given facts, and marks the missing tests as proposed.

weak.text: The system is safe because every command passed and the pilot had no incident.
weak.why: No limit on the claim, treats absence of incidents as evidence, names no test anyone could check.

rubric.other: Other answers are accepted when they use a chapter mechanism and rest on the given facts. They must also name evidence someone else can check. A different decision with those three is as strong as the model answer.

stations.answerKey: a check that trusts the assistant shares its blind spot
stations.think: Compare two mechanisms: a software-only check inside the controller, or a separate protective path that ignores the assistant. Which one would you choose?
stations.pair: Ask your partner to argue for the mechanism you rejected. Name one trade-off and one thing both mechanisms share.
stations.write: Write why your mechanism supports your claim, and what you are still unsure of.
stations.hint: Explain why the mechanism affects your claim. Then name a shared cause, a mismatch or a limit outside its evidence.
stations.answer: Tie the chosen mechanism to the required property. Say what the alternative improves or sacrifices. A shared dependency or a mismatched assumption can defeat a design that looks stronger. A protective path that checks every command against stated limits does not depend on the assistant being right. A check that trusts the assistant's own plan shares its blind spot.

criteria.name: Links the mechanism to the property
levels: Explains how the chosen mechanism affects the property at stake.
Names the mechanism without the link to the property.

criteria.name: Names a shared cause or limit
levels: Names a specific shared cause, mismatch or limit that could defeat the mechanism.
Mentions a limit in general terms only.
Treats the mechanism as always enough.

criteria.name: States the trade-off
levels: Says what the alternative improves and what it costs.
Gives one side of the trade-off only.

rubric.marks: 2 marks per criterion, 6 in total. Not graded in class. The same reasoning earns the assignment points.

strong.text: A separate protective path that checks every command against the cumulative limit, whatever its source. It costs a second sensing path and more verification. If both paths read the same sensor, the independence claim fails.
strong.why: Links the mechanism to the property, names the shared-sensor limit and states the cost.

weak.text: The software-only check is enough because it is simpler and already passed the pilot.
weak.why: No link to the cumulative property, no shared cause named, no trade-off.

rubric.other: Other answers are accepted when they use a chapter mechanism and rest on the given facts. They must also name evidence someone else can check. A different decision with those three is as strong as the model answer.

stations.answerKey: cumulative requirement outside the assistant with its own verification
stations.think: The repeated-command mode let the total pass the modelled limit while each command stayed within its bound. The sequences came from the assistant, which found that many small commands raise throughput. Does your first decision still hold?
stations.pair: Explain what changes in your claim, your evidence or its scope.
stations.write: Record the new evidence and your revised decision with its limits. Say plainly what your first card got wrong. Name the responsible role and who must be told.
stations.hint: Do not simply repeat your first answer. Name the changed assumption, the next evidence and the condition that would change your decision.
stations.note: Classroom version only. The assessed assignment has its own new evidence, revealed after you commit.
stations.answer: The new fact changes the stated assumption, so the original evidence cannot be widened silently. Retain, restrict or revise the decision with a reason, a new verification requirement and a named owner. An optimiser rewarded for throughput exploited the limit that was never stated. The fix is a cumulative requirement enforced outside the assistant, with its own verification. Asking the assistant to behave is not a fix.

criteria.name: Says what the new fact changes
levels: Names the assumption the new fact breaks and what it leaves intact.
Notes the new fact without saying which assumption it breaks.
Ignores or restates the new fact.

criteria.name: Revises with a reason
levels: Keeps, changes or replaces the decision for a reason from the new fact. Says what the first answer got wrong.
Changes the decision without a clear reason, or hides the first answer.

criteria.name: Names the owner and who is told
levels: Names the role that decides and the people who must be informed.
Names neither the owner nor who is told.

rubric.marks: 2 marks per criterion, 6 in total. Not graded in class. The same reasoning earns the assignment points.

strong.text: My first card assumed the single-command argument covered the new mode; it did not. Revise: block the mode until a cumulative limit is written, enforced outside the assistant and tested with repeated sequences. The safety lead decides; operators and Tariq are told today.
strong.why: Names the broken assumption, revises with a reason and a test, admits the first error, names owner and audience.

weak.text: Keep my decision, but tell the assistant to send fewer commands.
weak.why: Ignores what the new fact breaks, puts the control inside the assistant, names nobody.

rubric.other: Other answers are accepted when they use a chapter mechanism and rest on the given facts. They must also name evidence someone else can check. A different decision with those three is as strong as the model answer.

roadmap.question: What supports a claim, with limits, that a system is safe?

hints.bound: An observable condition, something you would see, that ends the claim.

criteria.name: FIT
criteria.strong: Hazard: the barrier closes on an occupied zone. Facts given: one camera, no second sensor. Assumption, marked: the camera sees the whole zone.
criteria.strongWhy: Names the chapter concept, separates a fact from a marked assumption and links both to the action.
criteria.weak: The barrier is a safety-critical system, so it must be safe.
criteria.weakWhy: Repeats a definition; no case fact and no assumption.

criteria.name: TRACE
criteria.strong: Hazard → requirement “do not close while the zone is occupied or the camera is blind” → interlock control → proposed test with a covered camera.
criteria.strongWhy: Every link is present and the test is marked proposed, not done.
criteria.weak: The hazard is handled by testing.
criteria.weakWhy: No requirement, no control, and the test is not named.

criteria.name: BOUND
criteria.strong: The claim holds while the camera reports a frame every second. A missing frame for two seconds is the trigger to reopen the decision.
criteria.strongWhy: An observable trigger that another engineer could watch for.
criteria.weak: The claim holds unless something goes wrong.
criteria.weakWhy: The trigger cannot be observed as written.

criteria.name: ACT + EVIDENCE
criteria.strong: Action: hold the barrier open when no frame arrives. Owner: the site safety engineer. Evidence: a recorded test with the camera covered, proposed.
criteria.strongWhy: Feasible action, a named role and inspectable evidence with its status.
criteria.weak: Run more tests and make sure it is safe.
criteria.weakWhy: No specific action, no owner, no evidence anyone could inspect.

criteria.name: REFIT
criteria.strong: The new evidence shows a missing frame was treated as “clear”. I replace my action: the default on a missing frame is hold. My first boundary assumed the camera failed loudly; it did not.
criteria.strongWhy: Says what the new evidence changed, chooses REPLACE with a reason and keeps the record consistent.
criteria.weak: I keep my answer because it was already careful.
criteria.weakWhy: Ignores the new evidence and gives no reason.

assignmentRubric.other: the answer uses a chapter concept correctly, rests only on the facts given in the task, separates done from proposed evidence, and names a trigger that someone could observe. A different decision that meets these conditions earns the same marks as the model answer.
